title: Osmocote Fertilizer: How Slow Release Feeding Works
metaTitle: Osmocote Fertilizer: How to Use It on Plants
metaDescription: Osmocote fertilizer is a coated slow release feed that lasts months in a pot. See how it works, which grade to buy, how to apply it, and when to skip it.
excerpt: Osmocote fertilizer is a brand of controlled release fertilizer. Each round granule holds nutrients inside a thin resin coat. Water slips in, dissolves the nutrients, and they seep out a little at a time for months. So one application can feed a potted plant for a whole season instead of a weekly feed. It is popular for orchids, ornamentals, nursery seedlings and container vegetables.

heroImage.alt: An open tub of slow release fertilizer granules like Osmocote, each bead coated to feed plants for months

blocks.text:
Plants in pots lose food every time you water them, because the water drains out the bottom and carries nutrients with it. That is why potted plants need feeding more often than plants in the ground.

A controlled release fertilizer like Osmocote fixes that by letting the food out slowly. This guide explains how it works, which grade fits which plant, how much to use, and when a cheaper fertilizer does the job just as well. For feeding plants in general, see our guide on [fertilizer for plants](/blog/fertilizer-for-plants).

Each granule is a small ball of fertilizer wrapped in a coat of resin. After you apply it, moisture passes through the coat and dissolves the nutrients inside. The dissolved nutrients then move out through the coat into the soil, slowly and steadily.

The speed depends mostly on temperature. Warm soil makes the granules release faster, while cool soil slows them. How much you water matters much less, so one dose behaves about the same in a wet week or a dry one. When a granule is empty, only the soft shell is left.

blocks.title: In our heat, expect the shorter end
blocks.text: The months printed on a controlled release bag assume a mild temperature. In the Philippine lowlands the soil in a pot is often warmer, so the granules empty sooner. If the label says three to four months, plan on about three.

The numbers on the bag are N, P and K, the same as on any sack. The grade you see most in local garden shops is the balanced 14 14 14. Other grades exist, some with added trace elements and a longer release time.

items.title: Measure by pot size
items.text: The label gives the amount for each pot size. Use a measuring spoon, not a guess, because too much still burns roots.

items.title: Mix in or scatter on top
items.text: When potting, mix the granules into the potting mix. For a plant already potted, scatter them on the surface and scratch them in lightly.

items.title: Water as usual
items.text: Watering starts the release. You do not need to water more than normal.

items.title: Mark the date
items.text: Write down when you applied it, so you know when the granules will run out and the next dose is due.

blocks.title: Do not stack it with liquid feeds
blocks.text: A pot that already has a full dose of controlled release fertilizer rarely needs a weekly liquid feed on top. Doubling up builds salts in the mix, which shows as brown leaf tips and a white crust on the soil.
Osmocote fertilizer compared with other feeds

blocks.caption: Controlled release and the usual alternatives
rows: Building soil in beds and pots

blocks.text: Controlled release fertilizer costs several times more per kilogram than ordinary sack fertilizer. In a pot, that does not matter much, because you use only a spoonful. On a hectare of palay or corn, it rarely pays. For field crops, splitting [urea fertilizer](/blog/urea-fertilizer) or [complete fertilizer 14 14 14](/blog/complete-fertilizer-14-14-14) over the season gives the same steady feeding for far less money. Read more in [foliar fertilizer](/blog/foliar-fertilizer).
When it is worth it, and when it is not

items: **Worth it:** potted ornamentals, orchids, nursery trays, rooftop and balcony vegetables, and plants you cannot feed every week.
**Not worth it:** large garden beds and field crops, where split sack fertilizer costs far less.
**Still needed alongside it:** good potting mix with organic matter, because coated granules feed the plant but do not build the soil.

blocks.text: Keep track of feeding with anee.io

Whether you feed with coated granules or with sack fertilizer, the hard part is remembering when you last did it. In anee.io, the [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar) dates each feeding for every lot or bed, and the inventory records what you bought and used. For nursery and vegetable growers, Anee, the smart farm technician, can look at a photo of a plant with yellow or burnt leaves and tell you in Tagalog or English whether it is hungry or overfed.

blocks.title: Never forget a feeding date
blocks.text: Put every fertilizer application on one calendar and track what each bed or lot used.
blocks.label: Start free

items.a: It is a brand of controlled release fertilizer. Its granules have a resin coat that lets nutrients out slowly, so one dose feeds a plant for months.
The label gives a number of months, often three to four for the common grade. In hot Philippine conditions it releases faster, so expect the shorter end.
Many orchid growers use a small amount of controlled release fertilizer in the pot. Use less than for other plants, because orchid roots are sensitive to salts.

items.q: Can I use Osmocote on vegetables?
items.a: Yes, for container and rooftop vegetables. In field beds, ordinary complete fertilizer and compost cost much less for the same result.

items.q: Should I put Osmocote on top of the soil or mix it in?
items.a: Either works. Mixing into the potting mix spreads it evenly. Scattering on top and scratching it in is fine for plants already potted.
